Honda Confirms 2028 Body-On-Frame Pickup Truck Derived From Mitsubishi's Triton
13 photos
Photo: Mitsubishi
Mitsubishi's Laem Chabang complex in Thailand is theoretically capable of churning out 420,000 vehicles a year. Said industrial estate produced roughly 170,000 vehicles in 2025, which is just around two-fifths of its capacity. Going forward, that empty space will be partly filled by a Honda-branded truck.
The larger of the two Japanese automakers recently signed a memorandum of understanding to sell a body-on-frame midsizer based on the Triton, with sales planned to start in 2028 for ASEAN markets. Will that Mitsubishi -derived Honda truck be sold in the United States and Canada? We don't know for sure yet, and chances are it won't because the Triton's underpinnings were not developed with North America in mind.
Honda intends to beautify its yet-unnamed truck with dedicated stylistic touches, meaning that everything under its body panels will be shared with the Mitsubishi. The larger partner calls the arrangement complementary supply, and certain numbers reveal a few background details behind this complementary supply.
From the standpoint of Mitsubishi, output at the Thai production complex slid from a little over 310,000 vehicles in 2021 to 170,000 in 2025. Part of that nosedive is attributed to the Triton, which dropped to 82,766 deliveries worldwide last year. By producing a badge-engineered truck for Honda, the agreement raises plant utilization.
Regarding Honda, the second-largest Japanese automaker after Toyota doesn't really have experience with body-on-frame trucks. The Ridgeline it produces in the US for North America is best viewed as a crossover posing as a truck, and a unibody at that. Developing a body-on-frame truck would have cost Honda a whole lot of money, and Honda knows how difficult it is to deliver a truly compelling midsizer from the poor-selling Kia Tasman for the Aussie market.
Photo: Mitsubishi Brazil Making only minor changes to the styling of the Triton also makes a whole lot of sense because Honda recently booked its first loss since going public in 1957. The reported $2.6 billion deficit is tied to an extremely poor electric vehicle onslaught and the collapse of its Chinese business.
Speaking of China, both Japanese brands are fully aware that Chinese newcomers have carved into their share across Southeast Asia. From this standpoint, it's easy to understand that Mitsubishi sees the Honda order as a way to enhance the bottom line. This memorandum of agreement dates back to an August 2024 merger plan that included Nissan.
Talks did collapse after Honda proposed taking full control of Nissan. Two years later, this pickup is the first tangible product of the surviving agreement. While the proposed merger is of no relevance anymore, the trading is. Honda is also weighing mutual vehicle supply with Nissan in North America, and rumor has it that body-on-frame models are of interest to Honda in this part of the world.
Could that mean the revived Xterra could also get a Honda-badged sibling? We'll have to wait and see, but that's easy to imagine. After all, even Nissan used Mitsubishi's Triton for its fourth-generation Navara. And just like Honda's mid-size truck for ASEAN markets, the 2026 model year Navara is related to the all-new Pajero. As The Weeknd once said during his mixtape era, this is a happy house, and we're happy here.
